note: The Sages said that Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai would take a myrtle branch and dance before a bride, calling out: A fair and attractive bride. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak went further and juggled three branches as he danced, and Rabbi Zeira complained that the old man was humiliating them. When Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak died, a pillar of fire separated him from everyone else, a sign the tradition says is given to only one or two people in a generation. Rabbi Zeira then said that the old man's branch had served him well; others report that he said his nonsense, or his method, had served him well.
why: The discussion has been collecting the songs sung to praise brides and newly ordained Sages; this story turns to how far a Sage may go to bring joy to a bride, and is followed by Rav Aha, who danced with a bride on his shoulders.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai
people.about: A Sage who danced before brides holding a myrtle branch.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak
people.about: An old Sage who juggled three myrtle branches while dancing before brides.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who first objected to the juggling, then said it had earned the old man his honor.

terms.meaning: A fragrant green branch, carried here as part of the celebration in front of the bride.
A heavenly sign of honor; by the tradition the Gemara cites, it marks off only one or two people in a generation.

note: Abaye's tenant farmer asked him whether he could betroth a nursing woman fifteen months after her child was born. Abaye said yes, piling up reasons: the law usually follows Rabbi Yehuda, the earlier school of Beit Hillel held the shorter wait, and Ulla and Mar Ukva had both permitted it. When Abaye told his teacher Rav Yosef, Rav Yosef quoted Rav and Shmuel: she must wait twenty-four months even before betrothal. Abaye ran three parasangs after the farmer (some say one parasang through sand) but could not catch him. He drew the lesson that one should not rule even on something as simple as eating an egg in a milk dish near one's teacher, because one will not get it right.
why: A teaching of the Sages says a nursing widow must wait before remarrying, with opinions ranging from 24 to 18 months; the story shows the shorter wait being relied on in practice and then overturned by Rav and Shmuel's stricter ruling.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who gave a lenient ruling to his tenant farmer and later regretted it.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who told him Rav and Shmuel required a 24-month wait.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A Sage who ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda's shorter wait.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: A Sage who said Rabbi Hanina allowed him to marry a nursing woman after fifteen months.

terms.meaning: Here, a widow still nursing her baby; the Sages made her wait before remarrying so a new pregnancy would not cut off the child's milk.
A Persian unit of distance, a long walk of several kilometers.
Two early schools of Sages that often disagreed; the law usually follows Beit Hillel.

note: Two deeds of sale for the same field came before Rav Yosef. One said the field was sold on the fifth of Nisan; the other said only that it was sold in Nisan. Rav Yosef gave the field to the holder of the dated deed, telling the other man that his deed could have been written as late as the twenty-ninth. The loser then asked for a court document letting him collect from land the seller sold from the first of Iyyar onward. Rav Yosef refused, because any buyer could answer: your deed may be from the first of Nisan, so the field you bought really is yours; go take it back from the other man.
why: The Gemara has just told of two deeds to one property written on the same day, where Rav Sheshet and Rav Nahman ruled differently; this is a further case of competing deeds, and afterwards the Gemara explains how the two holders could protect themselves.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The judge before whom the two conflicting deeds were brought.

terms.meaning: A written record of a sale; its date matters because the earlier buyer has the stronger claim.
A court document allowing a creditor or buyer to seize property the debtor had sold or pledged.
Land that stands as security for a debt, so it can be taken from a later buyer if the debt is not paid.

note: On the day Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was dying, the Sages declared a fast and prayed for him, threatening to stab with a sword anyone who said he had died. His maidservant went up to the roof and first prayed that those below would prevail over those above; but seeing him suffer, going in and out of the bathroom and taking his phylacteries off and on, she prayed the opposite. When the Sages would not stop praying, she threw a jug from the roof; in the moment of silence, he died. Bar Kappara, sent to check, told the Sages in a parable that angels had captured the sacred ark, leaving them to say the word themselves. As he died, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi raised his ten fingers and said he had toiled in Torah without enjoying the world, and a Divine Voice answered: He enters in peace.
why: The Gemara has been discussing where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi lay ill, in Tzippori rather than Beit She'arim; it goes on to tell the day of his death, and afterwards explains the verse the Divine Voice quoted.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The great Sage whose death is told here.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: A Sage sent to check on Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who broke the news in a parable.

terms.meaning: Small leather boxes holding verses of the Torah, worn on the head and arm and removed before entering a bathroom.
A voice from Heaven announcing God's judgment.
Heaven, which wanted the dying Sage, and the people on earth, who prayed to keep him.

note: Rav Hiyya Arikha's mother-in-law was also his brother's widow. She lived in her father's house, and for twenty-five years he supported her from his brother's estate. Then he told her she had lost the right to both support and her marriage-contract payment. She took him to Rabba bar Sheila, who ruled that she had not claimed out of embarrassment at his respectful treatment, and ordered him to pay. When he refused, Rabba bar Sheila wrote her a document letting her seize his property, and Rava upheld the ruling. But when she asked Rava for the produce of that property, he found the document did not state that the land came from her late husband's estate, so it was flawed and gave her no right to the produce.
why: The mishna says a widow living in her father's house may always collect her marriage contract, but one in her husband's house loses it after twenty-five years; this case tests that rule on a widow treated with respect while in her father's house.

people.name: Rav Hiyya Arikha
people.about: Supported his widowed sister-in-law, who was also his mother-in-law, then refused to pay her marriage contract.

people.name: Rabba bar Sheila
people.about: The judge who ordered Rav Hiyya Arikha to pay and wrote her a seizure document.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who upheld the ruling but found the seizure document faulty.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, a document promising a wife a sum of money from her husband's property if he dies or divorces her.
Food and support owed to a widow from her late husband's estate until she collects her marriage contract.
A court document allowing a creditor to seize specific property in payment.
The crops and income a property yields, which belong to whoever owns it at the time.
